transcription.tex: \textbf{1.}\quad \(2,\ 5,\ 8,\ 11,\ 14,\ldots\)\par Name this type of sequence and describe the change between consecutive terms.
\textbf{Arithmetic sequence}\par Add the same amount each time: \(+3\).\par The \textbf{common difference} is \(d=3\).
\textbf{2.}\quad \(3,\ 6,\ 12,\ 24,\ 48,\ldots\)\par Name this type of sequence and describe the change between consecutive terms.
\textbf{Geometric sequence}\par Multiply by the same number each time: \(\times2\).\par The \textbf{common ratio} is \(r=2\).
\textbf{3.}\quad \(1,\ 1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 5,\ 8,\ldots\)\par How is each new term generated?
This is the \textbf{Fibonacci sequence}. After the first two terms, each term is the sum of the preceding two.\par This is a \textbf{recurrence relation}: new terms are defined using earlier terms.
\textbf{Definition}\par An arithmetic sequence has a constant difference between consecutive terms.\par Geometric sequences and recurrence relations will be explored later in this chapter.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Sequence notation}\par Consider\[2,\ 5,\ 8,\ 11,\ 14,\ldots\]
What does \(n\) represent?
\(n\) is the \textbf{position} of a term in the sequence.\par Positions start at \(n=1\).
What does \(u_n\) represent?
\(u_n\) is the \textbf{value of the term} at position \(n\).\par For example, \(u_3\) means the third term.
For the value \(8\), state its position and its term notation.
\[n=3,\qquad u_3=8.\]\par Do not confuse the position 3 with the value 8.

transcription.tex: \textbf{The general term}\par Let \(a\) be the first term and \(d\) the common difference.\par Moving to position \(n\) takes \(n-1\) steps.\[\begin{aligned}u_1&=a,\\u_2&=a+d,\\u_3&=a+2d.\end{aligned}\]\[\boxed{u_n=a+(n-1)d}\]\par Write down \(a\), \(d\) and the relevant position before substituting.

\[55-2n<0\Rightarrow n>27.5.\]\par The first integer position is \(n=28\):\[u_{28}=55-56=-1.\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{1. Find the constants}\par A sequence is generated by \(u_n=an+b\), where \(a\) and \(b\) are constants. Given \(u_3=5\) and \(u_8=20\), find \(a\) and \(b\).

\[\begin{aligned}3a+b&=5,\\8a+b&=20.\end{aligned}\]\par Subtracting gives \(5a=15\), so \(a=3\).\par Then \(3(3)+b=5\), giving \(b=-4\).\[\boxed{u_n=3n-4}\]\par Here \(a\) is the coefficient of \(n\), not the first term.
\textbf{2. Equal differences}\par For which values of \(x\) do \(-8\), \(x^2\) and \(17x\) form the first three terms of an arithmetic sequence?
Consecutive differences must be equal:\[\begin{aligned}x^2-(-8)&=17x-x^2,\\2x^2-17x+8&=0,\\(2x-1)(x-8)&=0.\end{aligned}\]\[\boxed{x=\tfrac12\ \text{or}\ x=8}\]\par Each value gives equal differences.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Edexcel C1 May 2014(R), Q10}\par Xin has a 14-day training schedule. She runs for \(A\) minutes on day 1 and increases her running time by \(d+1\) minutes each day, where \(A\) and \(d\) are constants.\par \textbf{(a)} Show that on day 14 she runs for \(A+13d+13\) minutes. (2 marks)
There are 13 increases between days 1 and 14:\[X_{14}=A+13(d+1)=A+13d+13.\]

Yi also has a 14-day schedule. She runs for \(A-13\) minutes on day 1 and increases her running time by \(2d-1\) minutes each day.\par \textbf{(b)} Yi and Xin run for the same time on day 14. Find \(d\). (3 marks)
\[\begin{aligned}Y_{14}&=(A-13)+13(2d-1)\\&=A+26d-26.\end{aligned}\]\par Equating the two times:\[\begin{aligned}A+13d+13&=A+26d-26,\\39&=13d,\\d&=3.\end{aligned}\]

\textbf{5.} A sequence is generated by \(u_n=pn+q\). Given \(u_6=9\) and \(u_9=11\), find \(p\) and \(q\).

transcription.tex: \textbf{STEP I 2004, Q5.} The positive integers split into five arithmetic progressions:\par \(A:1,6,11,16,\ldots\)\quad \(B:2,7,12,17,\ldots\)\quad \(C:3,8,13,18,\ldots\)\par \(D:4,9,14,19,\ldots\)\quad \(E:5,10,15,20,\ldots\)
Give the general term of each progression. Prove that any term in B plus any term in C belongs to E.

For positive integer positions \(n\):\par \(A_n=5n-4\), \(B_n=5n-3\), \(C_n=5n-2\), \(D_n=5n-1\), \(E_n=5n\).\par The positions may differ:\[\begin{aligned}B_n+C_m&=(5n-3)+(5m-2)\\&=5(n+m-1)\\&=E_{n+m-1}.\end{aligned}\]\par Since \(n,m\ge1\), the position \(n+m-1\) is positive.
Prove that the square of every term in B belongs to D. State and prove a similar claim for the square of every term in C.

\[\begin{aligned}(5n-3)^2&=25n^2-30n+9\\&=5(5n^2-6n+2)-1.\end{aligned}\]\par Thus \(B_n^2\) belongs to D. Also\[\begin{aligned}(5n-2)^2&=25n^2-20n+4\\&=5(5n^2-4n+1)-1.\end{aligned}\]\par Thus \(C_n^2\) belongs to D too. Both displayed positions are positive integers for \(n\ge1\).
Show there are no positive integer solutions:\par (i) \(x^2+5y=243723\).\par (ii) \(x^4+2y^4=26081974\).

\textbf{(i)} Modulo 5, squares have remainders 0, 1 or 4. Adding \(5y\) changes none of these.\par The right side has remainder 3, so equality is impossible.\par \textbf{(ii)} Modulo 5, fourth powers are 0 or 1. Thus \(x^4+2y^4\) can only be 0, 1, 2 or 3.\par The right side is 4 modulo 5, so equality is impossible.

transcription.tex: \textbf{What is a series?}\par A series is a sum of terms in a sequence. In this syllabus, a series may be finite or infinite.
\textbf{Arithmetic series}\par Add terms of an arithmetic sequence:\[2+5+8+11.\]\par Consecutive terms have a constant difference.

\textbf{Taylor series}\par Functions can be expressed as infinite series of powers of \(x\). For example:\[e^x=1+\frac{x}{1!}+\frac{x^2}{2!}+\frac{x^3}{3!}+\cdots\]\par This is studied in Further Mathematics.
\textbf{Terminology}\par A power series is an infinite series of increasing non-negative integer powers of a variable, with constant coefficients. Power series also appear in Further Statistics.

\textbf{Binomial series}\par A negative or fractional power can produce an infinite expansion. For \(|x|<1\):\[\sqrt{1+x}=1+\frac{x}{2}-\frac{x^2}{8}+\frac{x^3}{16}-\cdots\]\par This is studied later in Year 2.
\textbf{Partial sums}\par The harmonic series is\[1+\frac12+\frac13+\frac14+\cdots\]\par A partial sum uses a finite number of terms:\[H_3=1+\frac12+\frac13=\frac{11}{6}.\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{The sum of an arithmetic series}\par Let \(a\) be the first term, \(d\) the common difference and \(S_n\) the sum of the first \(n\) terms.
\[\boxed{S_n=\frac n2\bigl(2a+(n-1)d\bigr)}\]
\textbf{Exam note}\par Be able to explain this proof. Symmetrically opposite terms add to the same total; the forward-and-reverse argument works for both odd and even \(n\).

\textbf{See the pairing}\par Consider \(2,5,8,11,14,17,\ldots\). Write the first five terms forwards and backwards.\[\begin{aligned}S_5&=2+5+8+11+14,\\S_5&=14+11+8+5+2.\end{aligned}\]\par Add corresponding terms.
Each pair sums to 16:\[\begin{aligned}2S_5&=16+16+16+16+16\\&=5\times16=80,\\S_5&=40.\end{aligned}\]
\textbf{Prove the formula}\par Write the terms forwards and backwards, with \(L=a+(n-1)d\). Each corresponding pair has the same sum.

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=a+(a+d)+\cdots+L,\\S_n&=L+(L-d)+\cdots+a.\end{aligned}\]\par Each pair sums to \(a+L\), so\[2S_n=n(a+L).\]\par Substitute \(L=a+(n-1)d\):\[2S_n=n\bigl(2a+(n-1)d\bigr).\]\par Divide by 2 to obtain the formula.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Using the first and last terms}\par Suppose an arithmetic series has \(n\) terms, first term \(a\) and last term \(L\):\[a+(a+d)+\cdots+L.\]

\textbf{Pair the two copies}\par Write the terms forwards and backwards. Each pair consists of terms equally far from opposite ends, so each pair sums to \(a+L\).\par There are \(n\) pairs in the two copies together.
\[\begin{aligned}2S_n&=n(a+L),\\\boxed{S_n}&=\boxed{\frac n2(a+L)}.\end{aligned}\]\par The sum is the number of terms multiplied by the mean of the first and last terms.
\textbf{Connection to the earlier formula}\par The last term is \(L=a+(n-1)d\). Substitute this into the first-and-last-term formula.
\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=\frac n2\bigl(a+a+(n-1)d\bigr)\\&=\frac n2\bigl(2a+(n-1)d\bigr).\end{aligned}\]\par Both formulas give the same sum. Choose the one suited to the information given.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Edexcel C1, January 2012, Q9}\par A company offers two salary schemes for Years 1 to 10 inclusive. Scheme 1 starts at £\(P\), increasing by £\(2T\) each year. Scheme 2 starts at £\((P+1800)\), increasing by £\(T\) each year.
\textbf{(a)} Show that the ten-year total under Scheme 1 is £\((10P+90T)\). (2 marks)
First term \(P\), difference \(2T\), ten terms:\[\begin{aligned}S_{10}^{(1)}&=\frac{10}{2}\bigl(2P+9(2T)\bigr)\\&=5(2P+18T)\\&=10P+90T.\end{aligned}\]
\textbf{(b)} Both schemes give the same ten-year total. Find \(T\). (4 marks)
For Scheme 2:\[\begin{aligned}S_{10}^{(2)}&=5\bigl(2(P+1800)+9T\bigr)\\&=10P+18000+45T.\end{aligned}\]\par Equate the totals:\[\begin{aligned}90T&=18000+45T,\\45T&=18000,\\T&=400.\end{aligned}\]
\textbf{(c)} Scheme 2 pays £29,850 in Year 10. For this value of \(T\), find \(P\). (3 marks)
The tenth term is the first plus nine increases:\[\begin{aligned}P+1800+9T&=29850,\\P+1800+3600&=29850,\\P&=24450.\end{aligned}\]\par Scheme 1 therefore starts at £24,450.

transcription.tex: \textbf{3.} Find the sum of the first 50 even numbers.

The first 50 positive even numbers are \(2,4,6,\ldots,100\).\par Here \(a=2,\ d=2,\ n=50\).\[\begin{aligned}S_{50}&=\frac{50}{2}\bigl(2\times2+49\times2\bigr)\\&=25\times102\\&=\boxed{2550}.\end{aligned}\]
\textbf{4.} Find the least number of terms for \(7+12+17+22+27+\cdots\) to exceed 1000.

\(a=7,\ d=5\), so \(S_n=\frac n2(5n+9)\).\[\begin{aligned}S_n>1000&\iff5n^2+9n-2000>0.\end{aligned}\]\par The positive root is \(\frac{-9+\sqrt{40081}}{10}\approx19.12\). Hence \(n\ge20\).\par Check: \(S_{19}=988\) and \(S_{20}=1090\). The least number is \(\boxed{20}\).

transcription.tex: \textbf{6.} The sum of the first three terms of an arithmetic series is 12. The twentieth term is \(-32\). Find the first term and common difference.

\[\begin{aligned}a+(a+d)+(a+2d)&=12,\\a+d&=4,\\a+19d&=-32.\end{aligned}\]\par Subtract the second equation from the third:\[18d=-36\quad\Rightarrow\quad d=-2.\]\par Then \(a-2=4\), giving \(\boxed{a=6,\ d=-2}\).
\textbf{7.} Prove that the sum of the first 50 natural numbers is 1275.

Write the sum in both directions:\[\begin{aligned}S_{50}&=1+2+\cdots+49+50,\\S_{50}&=50+49+\cdots+2+1.\end{aligned}\]\par Adding gives 50 pairs, each summing to 51:\[\begin{aligned}2S_{50}&=50\times51,\\S_{50}&=\frac{50\times51}{2}=\boxed{1275}.\end{aligned}\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{8.} Show that the sum of the first \(2n\) natural numbers is \(n(2n+1)\).

The series is \(1+2+\cdots+2n\), with \(2n\) terms, first term 1 and last term \(2n\).\[\begin{aligned}S_{2n}&=\frac{2n}{2}(1+2n)\\&=\boxed{n(2n+1)}.\end{aligned}\]\par Note that the number of terms here is \(2n\), not \(n\).
\textbf{9.} Prove that the sum of the first \(n\) odd numbers is \(n^2\).
The series is \(1+3+5+\cdots+(2n-1)\).\par It has \(n\) terms, first term 1 and common difference 2.\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=\frac n2\bigl(2+(n-1)2\bigr)\\&=\frac n2(2n)\\&=\boxed{n^2}.\end{aligned}\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{10.} The fifth term of an arithmetic series is 33 and the tenth term is 68. The sum of the first \(n\) terms is 2225.
\textbf{(a)} Show that \(7n^2+3n-4450=0\).

\[\begin{aligned}a+4d&=33,\\a+9d&=68.\end{aligned}\]\par Subtract to get \(5d=35\), so \(d=7\) and \(a=5\).\[\begin{aligned}2225&=\frac n2\bigl(10+7(n-1)\bigr),\\4450&=n(7n+3),\\7n^2+3n-4450&=0.\end{aligned}\]
\textbf{(b)} Hence find \(n\).

\[\begin{aligned}n&=\frac{-3\pm\sqrt{9+4\times7\times4450}}{14}\\&=\frac{-3\pm353}{14}.\end{aligned}\]\par Thus \(n=25\) or \(n=-\frac{178}{7}\).\par The number of terms must be positive, so \(\boxed{n=25}\).

\textbf{3. MAT 2007, 1J}\par For every \(n\ge1\),\[\begin{aligned}(n+1)&+(n^4+2)+\cdots\\&+(n^{10000}+100)>k.\end{aligned}\]\par Which follows?\par A: \(k<1300\)\quad B: \(k^2<101\)\par C: \(k\ge101^{10000}\)\par D: \(k<5150\)

transcription.tex: \textbf{AEA 2010, Q2}\par An arithmetic series has \(S_p=q\) and \(S_q=p\), where \(p,q>0\) are distinct integers. Find its common difference \(d\), first term \(a\) and \(S_{p+q}\).
\textbf{(a) Common difference}

\[\begin{aligned}\frac{2q}{p}&=2a+(p-1)d,\\\frac{2p}{q}&=2a+(q-1)d.\end{aligned}\]\par Subtract:\[\begin{aligned}(p-q)d&=\frac{2(q^2-p^2)}{pq},\\d&=-\frac{2(p+q)}{pq}.\end{aligned}\]\par Cancellation is valid since \(p\ne q\).
\textbf{(b) First term}
From the first sum equation:\[2a=\frac{2q}{p}-(p-1)d.\]\par Substitute \(d\):\[\begin{aligned}a&=\frac qp+\frac{(p-1)(p+q)}{pq}\\&=\frac{p^2+pq+q^2-p-q}{pq}.\end{aligned}\]
\textbf{(c) Sum to \(p+q\) terms}
\[S_{p+q}=\frac{p+q}{2}\bigl(2a+(p+q-1)d\bigr).\]\par Substituting the values from (a) and (b), the bracket simplifies to\[\frac{-2pq}{pq}=-2.\]\par Therefore\[\boxed{S_{p+q}=-(p+q)}.\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{Compare the two sequences}\par Identify the type of sequence and its constant step.
An \textbf{arithmetic sequence}.\par Add 3 each time:\[d=5-2=8-5=\boxed{3}.\]\par The constant step is the \textbf{common difference}, \(d\).
A \textbf{geometric sequence}.\par Multiply by 2 each time:\[r=\frac63=\frac{12}{6}=\boxed{2}.\]\par The constant multiplier is the \textbf{common ratio}, \(r\).
\textbf{Definition}\par A geometric sequence is one in which each term is obtained by multiplying the previous term by the same constant ratio.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Textbook example}\par The second term of a geometric sequence is 4 and the fourth term is 8. Its common ratio is positive. Find the exact values of the common ratio, the first term and the tenth term.
\textbf{(a) Common ratio}

\[\begin{aligned}u_2=4&\Rightarrow ar=4,\\u_4=8&\Rightarrow ar^3=8.\end{aligned}\]\par Divide the second equation by the first:\[r^2=2\quad\Rightarrow\quad\boxed{r=\sqrt2}.\]\par Choose the positive root as stated.
\textbf{(b) First term}
\[\begin{aligned}a&=\frac4r\\&=\frac4{\sqrt2}\\&=\boxed{2\sqrt2}.\end{aligned}\]
\textbf{(c) Tenth term}
\[\begin{aligned}u_{10}&=ar^9\\&=(2\sqrt2)(\sqrt2)^9\\&=2(\sqrt2)^{10}\\&=\boxed{64}.\end{aligned}\]
\textbf{Tip}\par Writing \(u_2=4\) first helps distinguish the second term from the sum of the first two terms.

transcription.tex: The first three terms of a geometric sequence are \(3,x,x+6\). All terms are positive.\par Find \(x\) and the tenth term.
\textbf{1. Find \(x\)}

Consecutive ratios are equal:\[\frac{x}{3}=\frac{x+6}{x}.\]\[\begin{aligned}x^2&=3x+18,\\x^2-3x-18&=0,\\(x-6)(x+3)&=0.\end{aligned}\]\par Thus \(x=6\) or \(x=-3\). All terms are positive, so \(\boxed{x=6}\).
\textbf{2. Find the tenth term}
\[a=3,\qquad r=\frac63=2.\]\par Use \(u_n=ar^{n-1}\):\[\begin{aligned}u_{10}&=3\times2^9\\&=\boxed{1536}.\end{aligned}\]

\(a=3\), \(r=2\), so \(u_n=3\times2^{n-1}\).\[\begin{aligned}3\times2^{n-1}&>10^6,\\2^{n-1}&>\frac{10^6}{3},\\n-1&>\frac{\log(10^6/3)}{\log2},\\n&>19.3466\ldots\end{aligned}\]\par The smallest integer satisfying this is \(\boxed{n=20}\).

transcription.tex: \textbf{1.} A geometric sequence has only positive terms. Its third term is 20 and its fifth term is 80. Find the twentieth term.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Arithmetic series}
\[S_n=\frac n2\bigl(2a+(n-1)d\bigr).\]
\textbf{Geometric series}
\[S_n=\frac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}\quad(r\ne1).\]\par If \(r=1\), every term is \(a\), so \(S_n=na\).
\textbf{Proof of the geometric-series formula}\par Write the sum, multiply by \(r\), then subtract.

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=a+ar+ar^2+\cdots+ar^{n-1},\\rS_n&=ar+ar^2+ar^3+\cdots+ar^n.\end{aligned}\]\par All the shared terms cancel:\[\begin{aligned}S_n-rS_n&=a-ar^n,\\(1-r)S_n&=a(1-r^n),\\S_n&=\frac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}\quad(r\ne1).\end{aligned}\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{What happens to each running total?}\par A series converges if its partial sums approach a finite limit. Otherwise it diverges.
\textbf{1.}\quad \(1+2+4+8+16+\cdots\)
\textbf{Divergent.} The partial sums grow without bound.
\textbf{Divergent.} Odd partial sums are \(1,2,3,\ldots\); even partial sums are \(-1,-2,-3,\ldots\). They do not approach one limit.
\textbf{Convergent.} The partial sums approach \(2\).
\textbf{Beyond the A level syllabus — for interest}\par \textbf{4.} The harmonic series:\[1+\frac12+\frac13+\frac14+\cdots\]
\textbf{Divergent.} Its partial sums grow without bound, despite the individual terms tending to zero.

\textbf{Convergent.} The sum is \(\frac{\pi^2}{6}\).

transcription.tex: \textbf{Compare two geometric series}\par \(1+0.5+0.25+\cdots\) converges to 2, whereas \(1+2+4+\cdots\) grows without bound.\par A geometric series with non-zero first term converges when\[\boxed{|r|<1}\quad\text{or}\quad -1<r<1.\]
What happens to \(r^n\) as \(n\to\infty\) when \(|r|<1\)?
\[r^n\longrightarrow0.\]\par For example, \((\frac12)^{100000}\) is extremely close to zero. Negative ratios with \(|r|<1\) also tend to zero, alternating in sign.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Two ways to define a sequence}
\textbf{Position-to-term rule}\[u_n=2n^2+3\]\par Substitute the position \(n\) to find any term directly.
\textbf{Term-to-term rule}\[u_{n+1}=2u_n+4,\qquad u_1=3\]\par Double the previous term, then add 4. This is a \textbf{recurrence relation}.
\textbf{An initial value is essential.}\par A recurrence describes how to move between terms. The starting value determines which sequence it generates.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Edexcel C1 May 2013 (R), Q6}\[x_1=1,\qquad x_{n+1}=x_n^2-kx_n\quad(n\ge1).\]\par Here \(k\) is constant. (a) Find \(x_2\). (b) Show that \(x_3=1-3k+2k^2\).\par Given \(x_3=1\), (c) find \(k\); (d) find \(\sum_{n=1}^{100}x_n\).

(a) Show that \(S_4\) adds 36 squares of side \(a/27\).\par (b) Show that \(P_2=20a/3\) and \(P_3=28a/3\).\par (c) Find the perimeter \(P_n\).
